Introduction
Free radicals, including reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/NOS), are formed in the human body as a result of oxidative
metabolism, i.e., as a result of the many chemical reactions and metabolic processes that occur in the body and also have numerous
beneﬁcial functions (Fig. 1). Free radicals are capable of modifying important molecules such as DNA, lipids, and proteins, and
therefore affecting their ability to function or causing them to function abnormally. These processes are often referred to as oxidative
damage. Antioxidants have the ability to scavenge and neutralize free radicals, or are necessary to enable other molecules to perform
such a function. The body’s antioxidant system is complex and consists of various intracellular and extracellular, endogenous and
exogenous, and aqueous and lipid-soluble components that act in concert to prevent formation of ROS and terminate chains of
ROS-initiated peroxidation of biological substrates. Antioxidants present in the diet include vitamin C, vitamin E, carotenoids
and polyphenols. Metals and minerals that are key components of antioxidant enzymes, such as zinc or selenium, are also referred
to as antioxidants. Many antioxidants can also act as pro-oxidants in certain conditions, such as the presence of transition metals or
at high concentrations. Intervention studies demonstrating higher risk of cancer in smokers with b-carotene supplementation have,
for example, attributed this ﬁnding to its pro-oxidant effect (see section on b-Carotene).
